body_text: Rocky Mountain Chocolate Factory Reports Fiscal First Quarter 2027 Financial Results July 14, 2026 4:05pm EDT Download as PDF Related Documents 10-Q Filing PDF HTML XBRL ZIP DURANGO, Colo., July 14, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Rocky Mountain Chocolate Factory, Inc. (Nasdaq: RMCF) (the “Company” or “RMCF”), America’s Chocolatier® since 1981, is reporting financial and operating results for its first quarter fiscal 2027, which ended May 31, 2026. “Since stepping into the Interim CEO role, I have been encouraged by the commitment of our team, the engagement of our franchisees and the support of our Board,” said Allen Harper, Interim CEO. “I want to thank Jeff for his leadership and recognize the work he, Carrie and the broader team have done to strengthen the foundation of the business, including the important progress made across pricing, production efficiency, ERP and store-level systems, franchisee ordering capabilities and customer engagement. While our first quarter results reflect continued near-term challenges, I believe we are entering a phase where execution, alignment and accountability will be critical." “Working closely with the Board and leadership team, our immediate focus is on improving production, strengthening fulfillment and distribution, pursuing higher-margin product opportunities and evaluating ways to address the Company’s debt structure and working capital at favorable terms. These priorities will guide us in the coming quarters as we focus on product quality, service and franchisee support to better position Rocky Mountain Chocolate Factory for sustainable growth. Most importantly, we want our employees, franchisees and customers to feel renewed energy around this brand. We are working hard to ultimately make chocolate fun again.” Mel Keating, chairman of the Board, added, “Al brings decades of leadership experience in consumer-facing businesses and a deep connection to the city of Durango, its people and this Company through his service on the Board and as one of the Company’s largest shareholders. His familiarity with our business, franchise network and strategic priorities allows him to lead from day one as the Company remains focused on disciplined execution and long-term value creation for shareholders.” Fiscal First Quarter 2027 Financial Results vs. Fiscal First Quarter 2026 Total revenue was $6.1 million for the first quarter of fiscal 2027 compared to $6.4 million in the first quarter of fiscal 2026. A 3% increase in Durango product and retail sales from price increases was offset by lower royalty and marketing fees under revised franchise agreements. Total product and retail gross profit was $0.2 million in the first quarter of fiscal 2027 compared to $0.3 million in the first quarter of fiscal 2026, reflecting lower packaged product sales. Total costs and expenses were $7.1 million in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, up from $6.5 million in the first quarter of fiscal 2026. The increase was driven by higher cost of sales, higher general and administrative costs tied to the franchise website and third-party delivery platform rollout, and higher retail operating costs with the increase from two to four company-owned stores, partially offset by lower franchise and sales and marketing costs. Net loss was $1.2 million or $(0.12) per share for the first quarter of fiscal 2027, compared to a net loss of $0.3 million or $(0.04) per share in the first quarter of fiscal 2026. EBITDA was $(0.6) million in the first quarter of fiscal 2027 compared to $0.2 million in the first quarter of fiscal 2026. The Company will not host a conference call in connection with this earnings release. The Company currently expects to host a conference call in connection with its fiscal second quarter 2027 results. About Rocky Mountain Chocolate Factory, Inc. Rocky Mountain Chocolate Factory, Inc. is a leading franchisor of premium chocolate and confectionary retail store concept. As America’s Chocolatier®, the Company has been producing an extensive line of premium chocolates and other confectionery products, including gourmet caramel apples since 1981. Headquartered in Durango, Colorado, Rocky Mountain Chocolate Factory is ranked among Entrepreneur’s Franchise 500® for 2026. The Company and its franchisees and licensees operate approximately 250 Rocky Mountain Chocolate stores across the United States, with several international locations. The Company's common stock is listed on the Nasdaq Capital Market under the symbol "RMCF." title: 10 Key Steps in the Modern Revenue Cycle Management (RCM) Process to Know in 2026
summary: Learn 10 modern healthcare RCM processes to boost collections, reduce denials, prevent revenue leakage, and streamline your revenue cycle operations.
body_text: Modern healthcare organizations operate in an increasingly complex financial environment, where rising patient financial responsibility, stricter payer requirements, and automated insurance solutions make revenue management more challenging than ever. In clinics and hospitals, effective financial management is critical to maintaining stability, as even small inefficiencies can lead to significant revenue loss. Common challenges such as claim delays, denials, manual errors, and inaccurate data entry continue to disrupt the billing process and create revenue leakage across healthcare systems. These interlinked issues make it complex for healthcare organizations to sustain steady financial performance. This is where revenue cycle management (RCM) plays a vital role. RCM serves as an end-to-end solution that streamlines billing, coding, claims processing, and collections. It connects clinical services directly with financial outcomes, ensuring that every patient interaction is accurately captured and efficiently converted into revenue. Discover how leading revenue cycle management companies achieve comprehensive growth goals that go beyond costs and bottom lines. Download the e-book: 8 Proven Strategies for Growing your Revenue Cycle Management Company What is Revenue Cycle Management in Healthcare ? Revenue cycle management (RCM) is the end-to-end financial process that governs how healthcare providers capture, manage, and collect revenue for services delivered to patients. RCM covers the full patient financial journey, from the moment a patient schedules an appointment through registration, eligibility verification, clinical documentation, charge capture, coding, claim submission, payer adjudication, payment posting, denial management, and final patient balance collection. In healthcare practice, the revenue cycle is not a linear process but a connected financial solution where each stage impacts the next. Errors in early steps, such as patient registration or eligibility checks, can lead to claim denials, delays, and increased administrative costs later in the cycle. Revenue cycle management (RCM) plays a critical role in healthcare organizations by ensuring financial stability and operational efficiency. It is used across the industry, including hospitals, clinics, and solo or independent practices to manage reimbursements and maintain consistent cash flow. Revenue cycle management (RCM) is one of the most important aspects of healthcare operations, as it reduces inefficiencies, minimizes revenue leakage, and streamlines financial workflows to help healthcare providers maintain stronger financial performance and operational stability. Importance of Revenue Cycle Management ( R CM ) A well optimized revenue cycle management (RCM) process ensures: Stable and Predictable Cash Flow Reduced Revenue Leakage Across All Stages Improved Billing Accuracy and Compliance Alignment Lower Claim Denial Rates Increased Operational Efficiency Better Financial Transparency and Reporting Accuracy In modern healthcare systems, revenue cycle management (RCM) is the only option. It supports financial stability, improves operational efficiency, and helps organizations stay sustainable over the long term. 10 Key Steps in Revenue Cycle Management (RCM) Process 1. Patient Scheduling and Registration It is the fundamental stage of the revenue cycle management (RCM) process, where all insurance, demographic, and contact information are gathered before care delivery begins. This stage instantly influences the value of downstream billing results. Precise insurance validation, demographic precision, or patient identity are crucial because any discrepancy here propagates into delayed reimbursement or claim rejection in the cycle. From a financial perspective, patient scheduling and preregistration serve as the first checkpoint for protecting revenue integrity. Errors at this stage often lead to claim denials that require expensive rework or complete resubmission, increasing administrative cost per claim significantly. In 2026, leading organizations are increasingly relying on automated intake systems, real time data validation, and EHR integrated registration workflows to reduce human error. Within advanced revenue cycle management (RCM) solutions , patient registration is no longer a manual administrative task, but an automated verification process that ensures clean data flow into billing systems. 2. Insurance Eligibility Verification Insurance eligibility verification ensures that a patient’s coverage is active, and that services planned are reimbursable under their payer’s plan. This step has become financially critical due to the rise of high deductible health plans and more restrictive payer policies. When eligibility is not verified upfront, providers face higher rates of denied claims and increased patient responsibility balances. A failure in eligibility verification leads to immediate revenue disruption. Claims may be rejected due to inactive coverage, incorrect payer information, or unmet plan requirements. Modern healthcare billing workflow solutions now use real time eligibility checks integrated directly into scheduling and intake platforms. This reduces manual verification delays and improves first pass claim acceptance rates. Integrated platforms incorporate eligibility verification into the front end of the medical billing process, ensuring that financial risks are identified before services are delivered rather than after claims are submitted. 3. Charge Capture The process of documenting all billable clinical services delivered throughout patient care is referred to as charge capture. When clinical services are not properly captured, they end up in immediate revenue loss and cannot be billed. Today, charge capture failure is one of the major sources of unseen revenue leakage in healthcare ecosystems. Reimbursement per patient encounter can be reduced by missing procedures, delayed charge entry, or undocumented services. In 2026, automated charge capture systems are integrated with electronic health records (EHRs) to reduce dependency on manual data entry. These systems ensure that clinical documentation automatically translates into billable events, improving accuracy, and reducing missed revenue opportunities. 4. Medical Billing and Coding It is the procedure of transferring clinical documentation into consistent billing codes, for example, CPT, ICD-10, and HCPCS. Payer reimbursement completely relies on coding accuracy, which is why it is important. Claim denials, compliance audits, or underpayments can also be the result of these minor errors. Inaccurate coding not only delays reimbursement but can also trigger regulatory risk exposure under CMS and payer audit frameworks. As healthcare shifts toward value-based care models, coding accuracy is becoming even more important for quality-based reimbursement alignment. Modern RCM solutions that incorporate specialized medical coding services increasingly rely on AI-assisted coding validation tools to reduce human error, improve compliance, and support accurate claim submissions. 5. Claim Scrubbing and Submission Claim submission involves preparing and transmitting coded claims to insurance payers through electronic clearinghouses. This stage determines how quickly revenue enters the reimbursement pipeline. Clean, error free claims significantly improve payment speed and reduce rejection rates. Failures in claim submission often occur due to formatting errors, missing data fields, or mismatched coding structures. These errors delay processing and increase administrative workload. In 2026, automated claim scrubbing tools and EDI based submission systems are standard across advanced billing platforms . Integrated systems enhance submission accuracy by validating claims before transmission, reducing rejections, and improving first pass acceptance rates. Claim Rejection vs Claim Denial Aspect Claim Rejection Claim Denial Stage in workflow Front-end clearinghouse validation Post-adjudication payer decision Processing status Claim never enters payer system Claim processed but not paid Common causes Formatting errors, missing data, invalid codes Eligibility issues, coverage limits, medical necessity Correction effort Low (fix and resubmit clean claim) High (appeal or resubmission required) Revenue impact Delayed cash flow Direct revenue loss risk Industry RCM best practice Clean claim scrubbing before submission Denial prevention + automated denial management workflows 6. Claim Adjudication and Processing Claim adjudication is the process where insurance payers review submitted claims and determine approval, denial, or request additional information. This stage is heavily influenced by payer specific rules, contractual agreements, and regulatory requirements. The outcome of adjudication directly determines final reimbursement amounts. When claims are denied or partially approved, it increases downstream workload and delays revenue realization. Automation in adjudication prediction is becoming increasingly important in modern revenue cycle management process. Claim Adjudication Outcomes Outcome Meaning Revenue Impact Approved Claim accepted as submitted Full or partial reimbursement received Denied Claim not payable by payer Requires appeal or resubmission; revenue risk Pending / Additional Info Required Payer requests documentation Delays reimbursement cycle Partially Paid Only part of claim reimbursed Revenue gap requiring follow-up 7. Payment Posting Payment posting involves recording insurer and patient payments into the billing system and reconciling them with submitted claims. This step ensures financial transparency and accuracy in revenue reporting. Incorrect posting can lead to inaccurate financial statements and distorted revenue forecasting. Automation in payment posting, including electronic remittance advice processing, is widely used in modern systems to reduce manual reconciliation errors. 8. Denial Management Denial management is the stage where the platform identifies rejected or denied claims, finding out the root cause behind them and making sure they are accurate to be resubmitted. This is one of the most crucial stages out of them all, as it can slow down the reimbursement flow and increase the time to recover payments. The common reasons behind claim denials include coding errors, incorrect patient eligibility information, modifier or bundling issues, and missing prior authorizations. If not resolved in a timely manner, denials can increase administrative burden and accounts receivable (A/R) aging for billing teams. In modern revenue cycle management system, denial management workflows are often integrated with billing software to track denial patterns, flag recurring payer issues, and support faster claim correction and resubmission. This helps healthcare organizations reduce preventable denials and maintain more consistent reimbursement cycles. 9. Accounts Receivable Follow Up Accounts receivable (A/R) follow up focuses on tracking unpaid claims and ensuring timely reimbursement from payers. Delayed accounts receivable (A/R) cycles reduce cash flow stability and increase financial uncertainty. Organizations with poor account receivable (A/R) performance often struggle with liquidity issues even when revenue volume is high. Automation tools now prioritize aging claims, flag high risk accounts, and trigger escalation workflows to improve recovery timelines. 10. Patient Billing and Collections Patient billing and collections involve invoicing patients for remaining balances after insurance payments have been applied. With rising deductible plans, patient responsibility now represents a significant portion of healthcare revenue. Inefficient patient billing communication can lead to delayed payments and increased bad debt. Modern medical billing services use automated reminders, flexible payment plans, and digital billing portals to improve collection efficiency while enhancing the patient’s payment experience. Conclusion In 2026, modern RCM solutions run as an interlinked financial network where organizational stability and revenue integrity are directly influenced by each individual stage of RCM processes. Healthcare practices accomplish more powerful cash flow, enhanced financial predictability, and reduced administrative burden when patient access, claims processing, denial management, coding, and collections run as a single system. CareCloud’s platform supports providers to revamp the whole medical billing workflow, enhancing financial performance outcomes, minimizing inefficiencies with the help of unified workflows and automation. In an increasingly complex healthcare environment, effective RCM results in smoother operations, long-term sustainability, and better financial health. Frequently Asked Questions 1. How does automation improve the revenue cycle management process? Automation improves the revenue cycle management (RCM) process by reducing manual errors, enhancing eligibility verification, optimizing payment posting, speeding up claim processing, and supporting faster reimbursement cycles with increased operational efficiency. 2. What is the average revenue cycle timeline in healthcare? Typically, a healthcare revenue cycle timeline ranges between 30 to 60 days, and it may vary depending on denial rates, payer responsiveness, and claim complexity. 3. Why is RCM important for healthcare organizations? Revenue cycle management (RCM) is important because it helps healthcare organizations maintain stable cash flow, reduce revenue leakage, improve billing accuracy, strengthen financial visibility, and support long-term operational sustainability. 4. Should healthcare providers outsource RCM ? Yes, outsourcing revenue cycle management (RCM) can help healthcare providers improve claim accuracy, reduce administrative burden, lower denial rates, and access specialized billing expertise. 5. What are the most important RCM KPIs? The most important revenue cycle management (RCM) KPIs include: Days in Account Receivable (A/R) Clean Claim Rate Denial Rate Net Collection Rate First Pass Resolution Rate Cost to Collect e-book: 8 Proven Strategies for Growing your Revenue Cycle Management Company Download Now

title: IA generativa: scrittura, editing e progettazione nel 2023
summary: I software di intelligenza artificiale generativa nel 2023 hanno raggiunto molti nuovi traguardi e i modelli di deep learning che generano immagini, testo, codice e altri contenuti sono ora prontamente disponibili per i consumatori. body_text: I software di intelligenza artificiale generativa nel 2023 hanno raggiunto molti nuovi traguardi e i modelli di deep learning che generano immagini, testo, codice e altri contenuti sono ora prontamente disponibili per i consumatori. Questa categoria di Intelligenza Artificiale (AI) sta trasformando il modo in cui gli early-adopters svolgono numerosi compiti ed è già stata utilizzata per scopi sia personali sia professionali. In questo articolo analizziamo la crescita della prima intelligenza artificiale generativa, OpenAI , e di altre due piattaforme straordinarie: Character.ai , che crea avatar virtuali per chattare e interagire, e il servizio di editing di video e foto facile da usare con diverse funzionalità intelligenti supportate dall'intelligenza artificiale, Wondershare.com . OpenAI ha svolto un ruolo cruciale nel promuovere l'intelligenza artificiale generativa nel mondo mainstream – un argomento che abbiamo analizzato in modo in dettaglio qui . L’audience totale del suo sito, Openai.com , è cresciuta del 127% nel 2023, infatti a settembre 2023 il sito ha registrato 102,8 milioni di visitatori unici nel mondo. Sia lo strumento di progettazione digitale di OpenAI , DALL.E , sia il suo generatore gratuito di testo e codifica AI, ChatGPT , hanno stimolato la condivisione di contenuti e la sperimentazione sulle piattaforme dei social media. Per esempio, tra molti contenuti, abbiamo visto l'influencer di Microsoft Mike Tholfsen condividere come sfruttare ChatGPT per le presentazioni di PowerPoint, l'influencer Karen X modificare DALL.E per ottenere risultati di design diversi. @mtholfsen Use ChatGPT to automate creating a #PowerPoint deck These are just simple ideas to get you started - have fun! #PPT #powerpointnight #learnontiktok #chatgpt #ai #officetips #Microsoft #hacks Monkeys Spinning Monkeys - Kevin MacLeod & Kevin The Monkey @karenxcheng I made a “music video” using AI to generate all images - using DALL-E 2 #dalle2 #artificialintelligence ♬ Feeling Good - Nina Simone Fonte: Comscore Social, Content Pulse, contenuti che menzionano "ChatGPT" o "DALL.E", su TikTok, 2022-2023 Cavalcando l’onda, altri strumenti basati sull'IA generativa hanno guadagnato popolarità e sono migliorati nel corso del 2023, come le piattaforme Character.ai e Wondershare.com . .ai sta ridefinendo la progettazione di chatbot e avatar, mentre Wondershare ha permesso di migliorare l'editing di video e presentazioni. Per comprendere meglio l'impatto globale dell'IA, ci siamo concentrati sui dati relativi a otto nazioni. Nel settembre 2023, il pubblico statunitense di Character.ai ha superato i 2 milioni di visitatori unici. In Messico, il numero si è avvicinato al mezzo milione, seguito rispettivamente da Regno Unito, Brasile, Francia, Spagna, India e Italia. L'analisi delle affinità di questa piattaforma rivela le tendenze degli utenti per età e paese. Gli utenti della Gen Z si posizionano ai primi posti dell'indice in quasi tutti i Paesi, soprattutto in Italia, dove la fascia d'età 18-24 anni ha registrato un impressionante 597 nell'indice di composizione UV* a settembre 2023 (5,97 volte più alto della media internet in quella fascia d’età). L'eccezione è la Spagna, dove l'audience 25-34 è 4,42 volte superiore alla media internet in quella fascia (indice di composizione UV* = 442). Per quanto riguarda l’audience di Wondershare.com , la piattaforma guidata dall'intelligenza artificiale ha registrato, in India, oltre 7 milioni di visitatori unici nel mese di settembre 2023. Gli Stati Uniti e il Brasile hanno superato il milione (rispettivamente 3 milioni e 1 milione di visitatori unici); anche il Regno Unito ha raggiunto un pubblico consistente, superando il mezzo milione di visitatori unici mensili nello stesso periodo. L'analisi delle affinità sottolinea la popolarità della piattaforma Wondershare tra i maggiorenni della Gen Z negli Stati Uniti, caratterizzata da un indice di composizione UV di 268, che si riscontra anche in Francia (150), Spagna (148), Messico (147) e India (136). Nella fascia di età compresa tra i 25 e i 34 anni la piattaforma è utilizzata in modo significativo in Spagna (194), Brasile (159), Stati Uniti (158), Italia (128) e Francia (107). È interessante notare che l’analisi di questa piattaforma AI mostra anche un'elevata affinità nella fascia di età superiore ai 35 anni. Nel mercato del Regno Unito, gli utenti di Wondershare.com con età superiore ai 35 anni sono 1,26 volte di più della media internet in quella fascia d’età, anche in Messico l’indice (104) mostra valori più alti della media. L'IA generativa nel 2023 sta rapidamente trasformando il modo in cui creiamo contenuti, soprattutto per la generazione più giovane. Con l'evoluzione di questa tecnologia possiamo aspettarci che un numero ancora maggiore di persone abbracci questi strumenti nuovi e innovativi negli anni a venire. Per saperne di più, contattate Comscore o visitate il sito comscore.com/learnmore. Definizioni: *L'indice di composizione UV confronta la proporzione di un profilo utente su un determinato sito con la proporzione di questo profilo nell'intera rete internet. Quindi, se un profilo utente corrisponde al 20% dell'audience di un sito ma rappresenta il 10% di tutti gli utenti di Internet, l'indice di composizione UV = 20% / 10% x 100 = 200 Ulteriori informazioni Artificial Intelligence Audience Measurement Demographics Gen Z Multi-Platform Social

body_text: View All News Speed Drives the Visit, Rewards Drive the Return, Vontier Survey Finds June 24, 2026 Download (opens in new window) New national research shows Americans are redefining convenience‑store loyalty around two expectations at once: faster, more seamless transactions and small rewards that deliver an immediate emotional payoff. RALEIGH, N.C.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- New national research from Vontier (NYSE: VNT) reveals Americans are quietly rewriting the rules of roadside retail. Consumers are reshaping the convenience-store visit in real time – demanding less friction and more value in the experience. New national research from Vontier shows Americans are redefining convenience‑store loyalty around two expectations: faster, more seamless transactions and small rewards that deliver an immediate emotional payoff. A survey of more than 600 U.S. drivers shows that nearly half (47%) of respondents want the ability to purchase snacks, beverages and everyday essentials directly at the fuel pump or EV charger. This marks the rise of Order at the Pump – the ‘Amazon‑ification’ of the forecourt, where every pump is expected to behave like a drive‑thru without the lane, the window or the wait. What used to be a quick errand is becoming a near‑instant interaction. But the story doesn’t end with speed. It begins with an interesting contradiction. Even as drivers look to bypass the store, they are not abandoning what the store provides. They want fewer steps, fewer delays and fewer interactions – but still expect the stop to feel rewarding, personal and worth returning to. Customers are separating the transaction from the experience and expecting both to be delivered in new ways. This duality builds directly on Vontier’s earlier research , which found that frequent visitors are motivated by identity – by feeling known, recognized and at home. The new findings show that identity and efficiency are not competing forces, but complementary expectations that C‑store operators must address. Today's consumers expect operators to cater to two distinct types of visits seamlessly: a fast, low ‑ interaction mode when they’re in a hurry, and a reward ‑ seeking mode where recognition and small perks matter. The operators who win will deliver both. Speed remains non-negotiable. Over 90% of drivers spend less than ten minutes on site, and 44% spend fewer than five. Reliability is equally decisive: seven in ten drivers say dependable payment and fueling systems are extremely important in determining where they return. Simultaneously, small, immediate rewards are rising in importance. More than half of drivers say free coffee or snacks make a loyalty program more appealing, with even stronger responses among Millennials and Gen Z. This dopamine perk signals that emotional rewards are becoming the new battleground for loyalty. Taken together, these trends point to a new model of convenience retail in which the forecourt becomes the primary interface for the entire visit: Transactions must be fast and nearly invisible; loyalty must feel instant, personal and emotionally rewarding; stops are becoming shorter; the car is becoming the checkout point; and the experience remains something customers want to return to. “Drivers are setting a new standard for routine stops,” said Mark Morelli, CEO of Vontier . “They expect the same speed and simplicity they get from digital experiences but still respond to the small details that make an in-store visit feel rewarding. The opportunity for retailers is to deliver both – fast, seamless transactions alongside experiences that customers actually look forward to.” The survey findings illustrate how these expectations are reshaping convenience store loyalty across visit behavior, transaction flow and rewards. Vontier’s portfolio of convenience retail and mobility technologies helps operators meet these expectations by connecting transactions, payments and loyalty across the forecourt and in‑store environment. By reducing friction at the pump and charger while enabling integrated rewards, Vontier solutions allow retailers to deliver faster visits without losing the elements that create repeat behavior. As convenience retail continues to evolve, the operators who succeed will be those who can resolve the central tension of the modern visit: making it shorter, simpler and more rewarding at the same time. title: Where Trust-Based Philanthropy and CSR Intersect
summary: Folding trust-based philanthropy into your CSR strategy will strengthen your community relationships and make your programs more resilient.
body_text: By nature, corporate social responsibility professionals face big, complex challenges. Their work is to channel corporate resources to solve society’s most pressing problems. And often they have to do so with limited budgets. They don’t have the time and resources to retread ground that’s already been covered. That’s why the most successful CSR professionals are the ones who can look out into the world and absorb the lessons other sectors have already learned—and then adapt those lessons to their work. In this regard, trust-based philanthropy is a test for CSR professionals. Essentially, private funders and nonprofits have learned important lessons about what’s at the heart of effective philanthropy. And the corporate sector needs to listen in. Because trust-based philanthropy is no longer an option, it’s becoming an essential pillar of corporate social impact. Trust-based philanthropy is rooted in relationships Trust-based philanthropy is a movement to make trust a core tenet of the relationship between funders and communities. It’s a course correction to the traditional mechanics of philanthropy, which have created startling power imbalances . Through trust-based philanthropy, funders put the decision-making power in the hands of their grantees, and follow their lead. In a recent interview , Pia Infante, co-executive director of the Whitman Institute and senior fellow of the Trust-Based Philanthropy Project describes how origins of the trust-based ethos started in 2009. She explains that, for nonprofits and community members, traditional philanthropy “creates an anxious power dynamic of ‘dancing for your supper.’” As with most grassroots movements, the shift toward trust-based philanthropy can’t be traced to one specific moment in time. It’s more a collection of efforts that have coalesced around a set of ideals. In describing the process of choosing the name “trust-based”, Infante explains that it was grantees who actually called out trust . “The truth is, if it had been just up to us, we probably would have called it ‘relationship-based philanthropy’—but we took the cue from our partners and ran with it,’” she says. Though trust-based practices have been percolating through the nonprofit and private foundation sector for a number of years, they’re now making their way into the world of corporate philanthropy. T. Rowe Price is a prime example. John Brothers, president of the T. Rowe Price Foundation has helped to pioneer a program focused on trust-based social good. “For us, what trust-based means is when we have the good fortune of being able to step into a local community, we recognize we are walking into somebody’s home. And we hold that ground sacred,” he says. John Brothers, President of the T. Rowe Price Foundation Brothers’ understanding of the sanctity and fragility of what it means to step into a community has helped him to redefine the philosophy behind corporate social responsibility. With his work, he proves that trust-based practices have the potential to transform CSR . Trust-based practices open the door to new opportunities The thing about adopting trust-based practices is that there is no simple checklist. Instead, using a trust-based approach requires you to interrogate every aspect of how and why your organization gives–and then reorienting to prioritize relationships. This process in itself has the potential to shift your CSR programs from a piecemeal effort to a thoughtful, coordinated, and long-term campaign for social good. Over time, it can transform your CSR programs into a pillar of your brand identity. Create effective solutions No one knows better what communities need than community members themselves. That’s why trust-based practices often lead to more effective solutions. When donors try to guess what communities want, they often miss the mark. John Brothers has seen this first-hand: “There’s a playground in West Baltimore that 15 companies came and built because somebody said, ‘hey, let’s go build a playground that should be a solution to unrest.’ And that playground has sat there unused for eight years. No community members ever asked for that.” When community members help direct funding, CSR professionals have a much better chance of creating programs that actually work. Funds go where they’re most needed. Plus, community members can help create programs that address the complexity and nuance of the ways social issues impact real people’s lives . Get community buy-in Community buy-in is a huge piece of the CSR puzzle. If community members feel like CSR programs ignore their identities and overlook their unique perspectives, it’s going to be difficult to get them on board—no matter what. Letting the community shape program priorities and design turns them into natural advocates. They’ll want your CSR initiatives to work just as much as you do. Shaady Salehi, director of the Trust-Based Philanthropy Project, explains what effective collaboration looks like : “It’s not just collaborating just for the sake of collaborating, but actually collaborating with the lens of humility, recognizing that we don’t have all the answers and curiosity where we can actually be open to learning from the grantee partners.” Build authentic relationships In the end, effective CSR hinges on strong relationships. And they cannot be relationships of convenience. You have to show up consistently, ready to listen and take ownership for the ways you’ve been complicit in perpetuating injustice. Brothers talks about the knee-jerk reaction many companies felt after the social unrest in Minneapolis: “20 companies in Minneapolis after the murder of George Floyd approached us and said, ‘Hey, look what’s happening in Minneapolis, like, we wanna have better relationships in our community.’ And what I said is the folks are not only upset that they lost George, who was their friend, their brother, their neighbor. They’re also upset at the conditions that were created that allowed that to happen—for which you were a part of.” Authentic relationships require you to explore some difficult truths about the ways your company has or hasn’t shown up in the past. And it’s not a one-time thing. You have to stay open to feedback about how the company’s choices—in business and CSR—impact community members. The main challenge: Letting go of “business as usual” Incorporating trust-based practices requires you to reimagine your role as a funder . You have to get accustomed to some discomfort as you shed old processes and craft new ones. And you’ve got to be mindful not to impose corporate frameworks where they don’t make sense. Grantees are not employees (or customers) Relationships with grantee partners don’t necessarily mimic other business partnerships. To build trust, companies have to let go of the notion that it’s their role to track and measure grantee performance. Brothers equates it to stepping into someone’s home. “If I walked into your home, and said, hey step on the scale and you should weigh what I think you should weigh,’ you’d tell me to get the heck out of your house—as you should.” Grantees should not have to prove their worth to their corporate partners. Instead, companies should let communities decide what success looks like and then support their journey to get there. Social impact doesn’t happen on quarterly schedule CSR isn’t like your other business initiatives. Its success cannot always be measured on a quarterly cadence. To get it right, you have to understand where your efforts fit into a long arc of social progress. Rather than imposing arbitrary timelines upon your programs, shape your timelines around what’s important to community members. Perhaps they feel urgency around some programs. Or they might know that certain efforts will take time to have an impact. Let them guide you on this front. Self-determination might feel new As much as funders have gotten into some bad habits, grantees have absorbed them too. It might take a concerted effort to help grantees get used to leading funders rather than following directives. Brothers says that this has been part of T. Rowe Price’s journey. Grantees were so used to funders making decisions, they sometimes craved that direction when it came to impact measurement. “We’ve had groups come in and say, ‘tell us what to measure.’ And we say, ‘we’re not gonna do that. We didn’t earn that right to do that. And as you sit before us, you represent thousands of community members that have put trust in you, and you’re just gonna give that to me? That doesn’t make sense. Let’s work on this together, honoring the position that you’re in and the position that I’m in. And let’s work together to figure that out.’” Aim to be a support system as your grantees learn how to identify what matters for themselves. Without that support and guidance, some organizations might never break out of their funder-focused mindframe. How to start your trust-based journey It’s easy to agree with the ethos of trust-based social philanthropy in theory, but the big question is how you start to fold those ideas into your work. 1. Start with your bedside manner The how of your philanthropy is just as important as the how much . “My advice to CSR and philanthropy professionals that are wanting to do this work well is start with your bedside manner and the how of your work,” Brothers says. “The very nature of the work after that is going to be that much better because you really spend time on how that work interacts with the community and its residents.” Approach your programs from the community’s perspective. Think about the ways you can prioritize relationships and honor individual experiences. As you work to establish or strengthen partnerships with community organizations, be sure you’re listening more than talking. 2. Break out of the savior dynamic Rather than asking community members what’s wrong in their communities, start with what’s working well. See if you can build programs around community strengths rather than focusing solely on their needs. In traditional philanthropy, there’s a tendency for funders to focus only on what communities lack. But this framing asks people to reduce themselves to their needs. “Communities don’t recognize themselves as needs,” Brothers says. “They recognize themselves much differently. The only way needs come in is by outsiders coming in and constantly talking to them about what’s wrong with them.” Retool your funding application to reflect this shift. If your application asks people to list all their hardships and failures without once asking about their successes, you’re setting the relationship up for failure. “I don’t know any service in the world that you can build off by asking somebody by building off of a glass, half empty,” Brothers says. Be sure to give applicants a chance to share their strengths, passions, and ideas alongside their needs. 3. Let go of arbitrary standards Philanthropy is often held to an incredibly high bar when it comes to transparency and accountability. The trouble is, sometimes those high expectations result in arbitrary standards. Funders make grantees jump through hoops or impose unnecessary oversight in the name of “impact.” For Brothers, breaking out of this dynamic required him to frame the investment in social good in a way his corporate leaders could understand. When they wanted to support specific projects rather than giving resources to an organization to spend how they wish, he explained that giving to a community organization was like investing in a brand. You wouldn’t invest in Diet Coke, the product—you’d invest in Coca Cola, the company, he reminded them. And you wouldn’t be in it for the short term, you’d want to focus on long-term return. Using this logic, he helped convince his leadership to take a long-term, trust-based approach to community investment. Be a champion of trust-based social good Championing trust-based practices as a CSR professional will make your community programs stronger and more resilient. Plus, you’ll have a hand in helping to reshape the whole philanthropic landscape to be more equitable and empathetic. The first step is finding a CSR software that helps you bring a trust-based philosophy into your day-to-day work. {{cta}}

title: Real-Time Insurance Verification: 71% of Practices Struggle
summary: 71% of dental practices say insurance verification is their #1 daily challenge. Discover how real-time AI verification cuts denials and boosts cash flow in 2026.
body_text: Why Real-Time Insurance Verification Is Breaking Dental Front Offices in 2026 If you asked 160+ dental billing professionals to name their single biggest daily operational headache, you might expect the answer to be claim denials, staffing shortages, or rising overhead. But according to the Group Dentistry Now 2026 RCM Report , the answer is none of the above. "Seventy-one percent pointed to insurance verification as their biggest daily challenge. Not collections. Not claim denials. Not staffing. Verification." — Foji.io, 2026 That number is striking — and it tells a story that every dental practice owner and office manager needs to hear. Insurance verification, a process that should be routine and predictable, has become the operational bottleneck that quietly undermines revenue cycles, strains front desk teams, and erodes patient trust. In this article, we'll break down exactly why manual verification is failing in 2026, what real-time automated verification actually looks like in practice, and how forward-thinking dental offices are using AI-powered tools to reclaim hours of lost productivity and dramatically improve their financial outcomes. The Manual Verification Problem: An Efficiency Paradox Front Desk Staff Are Drowning in Payer Complexity The traditional insurance verification workflow — calling payer hotlines, logging into multiple portals, cross-referencing benefit summaries — was already labor-intensive five years ago. In 2026, it has become genuinely unsustainable. Payer networks have grown more complex, benefit structures have become more granular, and the volume of patients with multiple or changing insurance plans has increased substantially. Front office staff are spending significant portions of their day on hold or navigating clunky payer portals, only to retrieve information that may already be outdated by the time the patient arrives. The result: claim rejections, patient billing disputes, and a front desk team that is perpetually reactive rather than proactive. The "Efficiency Paradox" Is Running Out of Room The 2026 Dental RCM Trends report from Zentist describes this situation as an "Efficiency Paradox." A strong 63% of practices are still collecting 90% or more of what they're owed — but they're achieving that only through intensive manual labor, not through operational efficiency. The system is being held together by sheer human effort, and that effort has a ceiling. Meanwhile, 78% of dental practices report an increase in claim denials or payer scrutiny over the past 12 months . Every denial that stems from an eligibility error — wrong coverage dates, lapsed benefits, incorrect coordination of benefits — is a direct consequence of verification data that was incomplete or stale. And with 58% of dental practices now committing to automation , the gap between early adopters and manual-process holdouts is widening fast. The Hidden Cost of Getting It Wrong Beyond claim denials, inaccurate insurance verification creates a downstream cascade of problems: Patient billing disputes when out-of-pocket costs differ from what was communicated at check-in Treatment plan abandonment when patients feel blindsided by unexpected costs Staff burnout from repetitive, low-value administrative tasks Delayed cash flow as A/R days stretch out while billing teams chase corrections 31% of dental practice respondents in the 2026 RCM Report cited rising patient out-of-pocket costs as the single trend most likely to impact their business performance. When patients are paying more out of pocket, they need accurate cost estimates upfront — and that starts with accurate, real-time insurance data. What Real-Time Insurance Verification Actually Means API-Driven Eligibility Checks in Under Five Seconds Real-time insurance verification isn't just "faster manual verification." It's a fundamentally different approach. Modern AI-powered platforms use direct API connectivity to payer networks, pulling granular eligibility data — co-insurance percentages, frequency limits, coordination of benefits, procedure downgrades, telehealth vs. in-person coverage — in under five seconds, without a single portal login. According to My Billing Provider's 2026 Automated Insurance Verification analysis , automated real-time verification achieves a first-pass claim acceptance rate of 94–96% , compared to just 70–78% for manual verification. Average days in accounts receivable drop to under 25 days, versus 45+ days with manual workflows. Those aren't marginal improvements — they represent a fundamental shift in how revenue cycles perform. Leading AI verification platforms can verify an entire day's patient roster in under five seconds, with connectivity to 300+ payers, according to DoctorConnect's 2026 review of AI insurance verification tools . Some cloud-based platforms connect to 1,000+ payers, including Medicare and all 50 Medicaid programs, as detailed in 314e's comprehensive guide to the top 18 insurance eligibility verification software solutions in 2026 . Batch Verification vs. Real-Time Checks: Understanding the Difference There are two primary modes of automated verification that practices should understand: Batch verification : Run automatically 24–72 hours before appointments, checking the entire upcoming schedule at once. This gives front desk teams time to address any issues before the patient arrives. Real-time point-of-service checks : Triggered at check-in to confirm that coverage hasn't changed since the batch run. Particularly important for patients with employer-sponsored plans, where coverage can lapse mid-month. The best platforms combine both approaches — running batch checks in advance and enabling real-time confirmation at the point of care. This layered strategy virtually eliminates eligibility-related denials. What Data Gets Pulled — and Why It Matters One of the most significant advantages of real-time API-based verification over manual portal lookups is the depth and accuracy of the data retrieved . A comprehensive real-time verification pull typically includes: Active coverage status and effective dates Deductible amounts (individual and family) and amounts met year-to-date Co-pay and co-insurance percentages by procedure category Annual maximum benefits and amounts used Frequency limitations (e.g., bitewing X-rays, cleanings, crowns) Coordination of benefits for patients with dual coverage Waiting periods for major services Procedure-specific downgrades or exclusions This level of detail allows front desk teams to generate accurate patient cost estimates before the appointment — a capability that directly impacts case acceptance and patient satisfaction. The Patient Experience Dimension: Why Transparency Wins Upfront Cost Clarity Is Now a Competitive Differentiator Insurance verification isn't just an internal billing function — it has a direct impact on the patient experience and your practice's competitive positioning. According to GetProsper.ai's Real-Time Insurance Eligibility Verification Guide , 75% of patients say that knowing their out-of-pocket costs beforehand influences their choice of provider . That's a remarkable statistic. Three out of four patients are factoring cost transparency into their provider selection — and real-time insurance verification is the operational foundation that makes that transparency possible. Practices that can confidently tell a patient "your out-of-pocket for today's crown will be approximately $340" before the appointment begins are building trust that translates directly into loyalty and referrals. Reducing Billing Surprises That Damage Retention Nothing erodes patient trust faster than a bill that arrives weeks after an appointment for an amount significantly higher than what was discussed at check-in. These billing surprises are almost always rooted in inaccurate or incomplete insurance verification. When a practice verifies coverage in real time and communicates costs accurately upfront, it eliminates the most common source of patient complaints and disputes. This is also where real-time verification connects to downstream revenue cycle performance. When patients understand their financial responsibility before treatment, they're more likely to accept treatment plans, make payment arrangements proactively, and return for follow-up care. The AI Patient Sales Coordinator from Patientdesk.ai builds on this foundation — using accurate insurance data to support treatment plan follow-up and case acceptance conversations that convert more proposed treatment into completed care. Real-World Outcomes: What the Data Shows Denial Rates Cut in Half — or More The business case for real-time insurance verification is well-documented. GetProsper.ai's 2026 guide highlights a compelling example from an orthopedic practice that implemented real-time eligibility checks: its denial rate fell from 11% to just 4% , and average time-to-payment dropped from 45 days to 26 days . While this example comes from orthopedics, the mechanics are identical in dental — and the financial impact is proportionally significant. A practice billing $2 million annually that reduces its denial rate from 10% to 4% is recovering an additional $120,000 in revenue that would otherwise require costly rework or be written off entirely. First-Pass Acceptance Rates That Change the Math The difference between a 70–78% first-pass acceptance rate (manual) and a 94–96% rate (automated) isn't just an operational metric — it's a financial multiplier. Every claim that fails on first submission requires staff time to identify the error, correct it, resubmit, and follow up. That rework cycle typically adds 15–30 days to payment timelines and consumes front office capacity that could be directed toward patient-facing work. My Billing Provider's 2026 analysis confirms that practices using automated real-time verification consistently achieve A/R days under 25, compared to 45+ days for manual workflows. For a practice with $200,000 in monthly production, cutting A/R days from 45 to 25 means approximately $133,000 more in cash on hand at any given time — a meaningful improvement in financial stability and operational flexibility. Choosing the Right Real-Time Verification Solution Key Features to Evaluate Not all verification platforms are created equal. When evaluating solutions for your practice, prioritize these capabilities: Payer network breadth : Look for platforms connecting to 300+ payers at minimum; enterprise solutions should cover 1,000+ including all Medicaid programs PMS/EHR integration : Seamless two-way integration with your practice management system (Dentrix, Eaglesoft, Open Dental, etc.) eliminates duplicate data entry Batch + real-time capability : Both modes should be available, not just one or the other Data granularity : Confirm the platform pulls frequency limits, coordination of benefits, and procedure-specific details — not just active/inactive status HIPAA compliance : All PHI transmitted and stored must meet HIPAA privacy and security standards; verify the vendor's compliance posture and BAA availability Automated alerts : The system should flag coverage issues proactively, not just return raw data HIPAA Compliance Is Non-Negotiable As noted by Wisdom's 2026 guide to insurance verification in dental RCM , HIPAA compliance is a critical requirement in real-time verification workflows. All communications and data storage involving Protected Health Information must adhere to HIPAA privacy and security rules. Practices should also re-verify coverage close to the appointment date, since employment or insurance status changes can invalidate earlier checks — a best practice that real-time systems handle automatically. Cloud-Based Solutions Are Dominating in 2026 Cloud-based verification platforms have become the dominant choice in 2026 for good reason: they offer scalability, automatic updates, and seamless integration with existing practice management systems without requiring significant infrastructure investment. According to 314e's 2026 software comparison , leading cloud platforms connect to 1,000+ payers and support both batch and real-time verification modes, making them suitable for single-location practices and large DSOs alike. Integrating Real-Time Verification Into Your Broader Automation Strategy Verification Is the Foundation, Not the Finish Line Real-time insurance verification is most powerful when it's part of a broader front office automation strategy — not a standalone tool. When verification data flows automatically into your practice management system, it enables a chain of downstream efficiencies: Automated patient cost estimates generated and communicated before the appointment Streamlined check-in with pre-verified coverage reducing front desk friction Faster claim submission with accurate eligibility data pre-populated Proactive denial prevention through eligibility alerts that trigger workflow corrections This is the vision behind Patientdesk.ai's real-time insurance verification and front desk automation features , which integrate directly with PMS platforms including Dentrix, Open Dental, and Eaglesoft to automate verification workflows alongside appointment scheduling, patient communication, and billing preparation. AI Receptionists and Verification: A Natural Pairing One of the most compelling integration opportunities in 2026 is pairing real-time insurance verification with AI-powered front desk automation. When a patient calls to schedule an appointment, an AI receptionist from Patientdesk.ai can capture insurance information at the time of booking and trigger an automated eligibility check — so by the time the appointment is confirmed, the practice already has verified coverage data in hand. This eliminates the common scenario where verification is rushed the morning of the appointment because the information wasn't collected or checked in advance. It also allows the front desk team to focus on the patient experience during check-in rather than scrambling to verify benefits in real time. The Market Is Moving Fast — and So Should You A $3.4 Billion Market by 2030 The scale of investment flowing into insurance eligibility verification technology signals just how significant this shift is. According to Research and Markets' 2026 Insurance Eligibility Verification Market Report , the market is projected to grow to $3.4 billion by 2030 , at a compound annual growth rate of 7.2%. The primary growth drivers are AI adoption, interoperability standards, and surging demand for real-time eligibility checks across healthcare settings. For dental practices, this market trajectory means two things: the technology is maturing rapidly, making it more accessible and affordable than ever; and the competitive gap between practices that automate and those that don't will continue to widen. Early Adopters Are Already Pulling Ahead With 58% of dental practices now committed to automation , the window for being an "early adopter" is closing. Practices that implement real-time verification now will consolidate the operational and financial advantages — lower denial rates, faster payment, better patient experience — while competitors still running manual workflows continue to absorb the hidden costs of the Efficiency Paradox. The question for practice owners and office managers in 2026 is no longer whether to automate insurance verification. It's how quickly you can make the transition — and how well you can integrate it with the rest of your front office and revenue cycle operations. Key Takeaways for Dental Practice Leaders Real-time insurance verification has moved from a "nice to have" to a genuine operational imperative. title: Veru Announces Full Enrollment for Phase 2b PLATEAU Clinical Trial of Enobosarm and Semaglutide Combination for High Quality Weight Loss
summary: -- Phase 2b PLATEAU clinical trial exceeds targeted full enrollment of 200 patients — -- Interim analysis results on track for calendar Q1…...
body_text: Veru Announces Full Enrollment for Phase 2b PLATEAU Clinical Trial of Enobosarm and Semaglutide Combination for High Quality Weight Loss July 27, 2026 8:10am EDT Download as PDF -- Phase 2b PLATEAU clinical trial exceeds targeted full enrollment of 200 patients — -- Interim analysis results on track for calendar Q1 ‘27-- MIAMI, FL, July 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Veru Inc. (NASDAQ: VERU), a late clinical stage biopharmaceutical company focused on developing innovative medicines for the treatment of cardiometabolic and inflammatory diseases, today announced the completion of enrollment in the Phase 2b PLATEAU clinical study to evaluate the effect of oral enobosarm 3 mg versus placebo on total body weight, fat mass, lean mass, physical function, bone mineral density and safety in ~200 older patients (age ≥ 65 years) who have obesity (BMI ≥ 35) and are initiating semaglutide treatment for weight reduction. The interim analysis results from the study are expected in the first quarter of calendar year 2027 with final topline clinical data expected in the fourth quarter of calendar year 2027. “We are extremely pleased to have expeditiously completed enrollment in the Phase 2b PLATEAU clinical trial, which marks an important milestone in the development of enobosarm as a potential next generation combination therapy with GLP-1 receptor agonists for older patients with obesity,” said Mitchell Steiner, M.D., Chairman, President, and Chief Executive Officer of Veru Inc. “There remains a significant unmet medical need in older patients with obesity who are more likely to have low muscle reserves to make weight reduction more tissue selective by maximizing fat loss while preserving lean mass, physical function, and bone mineral density for the highest quality weight reduction. Retaining muscle and preserving physical function burns more fat potentially enabling patients to break through the weight loss plateau to have greater weight reduction.” Dr. Steiner added: “Achieving greater than full enrollment across the study sites reflects the dedication of patients, investigators, healthcare professionals, and the Veru team. This accomplishment advances our mission to make the weight loss process as healthy as it can be, benefiting patients and making their lives better.” Veru Obesity Program: Evaluating enobosarm in combination with GLP-1 RA for higher quality weight reduction in older patients with obesity Fully Enrolled Phase 2b PLATEAU Clinical Study Phase 2b PLATEAU clinical trial is a double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the effect of enobosarm 3mg on total body weight, fat mass, lean mass, physical function, bone mineral density and safety in approximately 200 older patients (age ≥ 65 years) who have obesity (BMI ≥ 35) and are initiating semaglutide treatment for weight reduction. The Phase 2b PLATEAU study is designed to assess the ability of enobosarm treatment to break through the weight loss plateau observed in patients with obesity receiving GLP-1 RA treatment by preserving muscle mass and physical function to achieve clinically meaningful incremental weight reduction by 68 weeks. The primary efficacy endpoint of the study is the percent change from baseline in total body weight at 68 weeks. The key secondary endpoints are total fat mass, total lean mass, physical function (stair climb test), mobility disability assessment, bone mineral density, and patient reported outcome questionnaires for physical function, HbA1c, and insulin resistance. Results of an interim analysis assessing lean body mass and fat mass as measured by DXA after subjects have completed 32 weeks is expected in the first quarter of calendar year 2027. Final topline clinical data is expected in the fourth quarter of calendar year 2027. In June 2026 Veru announced a clinical supply agreement with Novo Nordisk for its Phase 2b PLATEAU clinical study*. Please see the Company’s SEC Form 8-K dated June 2, 2026 for further details. Completed Phase 2b QUALITY Clinical Study The Phase 2b QUALITY clinical study is a positive multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized, dose-finding clinical trial that evaluated the safety and efficacy of enobosarm 3 mg, enobosarm 6 mg, or placebo as a treatment to augment fat loss and to prevent muscle loss in 168 older patients (≥60 years of age) receiving semaglutide (Wegovy®**) for weight reduction. After the efficacy dose-finding portion of the Phase 2b QUALITY clinical trial was completed at 16 weeks, participants continued into a Phase 2b maintenance extension study where all patients discontinued semaglutide treatment, but continued receiving placebo, enobosarm 3 mg, or enobosarm 6 mg as monotherapy in a double-blind fashion for 12 weeks. The Phase 2b QUALITY and Maintenance Extension clinical trial was a positive study that demonstrated that enobosarm plus semaglutide preserved lean mass and physical function, and led to greater fat loss during the 16 week active weight loss period and enobosarm monotherapy prevented the regain of weight lost when the GLP-1 RA was discontinued. About Veru Inc. Veru is a late clinical stage biopharmaceutical company focused on developing innovative medicines for the treatment of cardiometabolic and inflammatory diseases. The Company’s drug development program includes two late-stage novel small molecules, enobosarm and sabizabulin. Enobosarm, an oral selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM), is being developed as a next generation drug that makes weight reduction by GLP-1 RA drugs more tissue selective for loss of fat and preservation of lean mass to improve body composition and physical function which is expected to result in clinically meaningful incremental weight reduction versus GLP-1 RA therapy alone. Sabizabulin, a microtubule disruptor, is being developed for the treatment of chronic inflammation related to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.
